script: "She vanished, I stole her plot—now the garden's secrets are killing us.". I had been tending my plot for almost four years, grinding dirt, sowing seeds, and watching green shoots pop up every spring. The board handed out plots, and if you didn't show up all season, the plot got reallocated. Two years ago, Diane's plot next to mine went wild—overgrown weeds, no tilling, no water. She'd bounced out of town for a family crisis, never replying to emails, so the coordinator labeled it abandoned. No paperwork changed because Diane was a ghost. I kept coming daily, so I asked the coordinator if I could clean it up and grow something there. He said yes, verbally. I pulled out the shovel, amended the soil, planted tomatoes, squash, herbs—nothing permanent, just annuals. Fast forward to this week: Diane pops back out of nowhere, having sorted everything with her family. She storms over, sees my tomato vines bursting with fruit, and loses it. "That's my plot," she screams, claiming all the crops belong to her because the plot is still officially hers. She wants the produce back. I am ready to hand over the plot, but the veggies—grown, watered, tended—are mine. I told her I'd give her the plot from now on, but the tomatoes? I am not giving them up. Now she's spreading the rumor that I am a thief, that I squatted on her land. The coordinator is stuck because no paperwork changed. Diane threatens to file a complaint. Some neighbors think I should have spoken to her two years ago instead of relying on the board's verbal nod. I am left wondering: did I cross a line by keeping my harvest, or am I the jerk for not surrendering everything when she returned? The stakes are real—my food, my reputation, the whole community vibe. I can't just hand over my tomatoes and say, "Fine, I am a bad person." That's not me. I am the one who grew this stuff, the one who worked hard. I am not a thief, I am a gardener. And I am not going to let a rumor ruin the hard work I've put in.
